name: Liko
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: de Wit, Gerrit. 2015. Liko Phonology and Grammar: A Bantu language of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. LOT Dissertation Series 411. Utrecht: LOT. (open-access PDF, lotpublications.nl/Documents/)
catalog_locator: ch. 4 'Tone', sec. 4.1 p. 121; also ch. 1 overview p. ~34; loanword adaptation sec. 5.x pp. 214, 216
catalog_quote: Liko is a tone language with two underlying tones, High (H) and Low (L). A tone is associated with a tone-bearing unit (TBU). A Low and a High tone can be combined on one TBU. Tone in Liko has a distinctive function, both in the lexicon and in the grammar. ... The syllable is the TBU in Liko. The language has only short open syllables containing one vowel. A vocalic segment in a syllable nucleus does not consist of more than one mora, which implies that it is not necessary to posit the mora as the TBU. ... [p. 214] Loanwords from Swahili have a single H tone in Liko corresponding to the stressed syllable in Swahili. ... [p. 216] Like in Congo Swahili loanwords, /r/ is replaced by [l] and the Liko reflex of the syllable with primary stress in French consists of a H tone.

new_statements.quote: En lika, il n'y a pas de voyelles longues contrastives aux voyelles courtes. La durée des voyelles peut varier dans la réalisation. L'allongement sur le même niveau tonale le plus sensible est appliqué si le locuteur veut accentuer ce qu'il dit. Autrement dit, la durée vocalique n'est pas distinctive mais expressive. [...] Le lika a deux tons sous-jacents: haut (H) et bas (B). Dans les noms avec la structure CVCV on trouve toutes les possibilités: HH, HB, BH, BB. [...] [n. 28, citing Casali 2004:] 2. Les voyelles dans la position pré-finale subissent un allongement sensible, surtout dans les mots avec la structure préfixe-CVCV.
new_statements.translation: In Lika there are no long vowels contrasting with short vowels. Vowel duration can vary in realisation. Lengthening on the same tonal level, quite noticeable, is applied if the speaker wants to emphasize what he is saying. In other words, vowel duration is not distinctive but expressive. [...] Lika has two underlying tones: high (H) and low (L). In nouns with CVCV structure all possibilities are found: HH, HL, LH, LL. [...] [n. 28, citing Casali 2004:] 2. Vowels in pre-final position undergo noticeable lengthening, especially in words with the structure prefix-CVCV.

new_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Les caractéristiques suprasegmentales', 2.1 'La durée' and 2.2.1 'Les tons H et B', p. 22 (p. 22), with footnote 28 on p. 22; tone continues pp. 22-27; syllable structure sec. 4 pp. 36-37; word structure sec. 5 pp. 38-40
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata: 43 pp., 'SIL Electronic Working Papers 2010-002, March 2010' on p. 2; clean text, extracted text used, no scanned). p. 22 carries printed footer '22' and holds all three quoted passages exactly as the compiler gives them: sec. 2.1 'La durée' opens 'En lika, il n'y a pas de voyelles longues contrastives aux voyelles courtes. La durée des voyelles peut varier dans la réalisation. L'allongement sur le même niveau tonale le plus sensible est appliqué si le locuteur veut accentuer ce qu'il dit. Autrement dit, la durée vocalique n'est pas distinctive mais expressive.'; sec. 2.2.1 opens 'Le lika a deux tons sous-jacents: haut (H) et bas (B). Dans les noms avec la structure CVCV…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's tonal-OR-pitch accent classification from de Wit 2015 (two-tone H/L system, syllable=TBU, depressor consonants, downstep, no stress rule): the 2010 paper, by the same author on the same central dialect, likewise posits H/L tone and no stress. It adds two compatible details the catalog lacks: (a) an explicit statement that vowel length is non-contrastive and purely expressive (p. 22), and (b) Casali 2004's instrumental observation, reported in n. 28, of phonetic penultimate lengthening in prefix-CVCV words. (b) is a phonetic-duration observation, not a tonal-penult rule, so it does not contradict de Wit 2015 p. 171 ('the penultimate syllable.. key role in Bantu tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper's suprasegmental chapter treats only vowel duration (non-contrastive, expressive; ideophones lengthened) and tone (two underlying tones H and L, all four CVCV melodies attested, minimal pairs such as káᵑga 'guinea fowl' vs kaᵑgá 'bed'; LH rising tone from prefix+vowel-initial stem fusion, verb-final vowel fusion, historical CVCV>CV loss, and depressor consonants /b, d, ɟ, g, g͡b, v, z, ʒ/; downstepped H before nominal suffixes). No word stress, accent or prominence rule is stated anywhere; a full-text search for accent/accentu/proémin/intensit/tonique/rythm/pénult finds only the tone-diacritic conventions ('accent aigu') and the expressive-lengthening remark. The only prominence-adjacent fact is footnote 28's report from Casali 2004 that the pre-final (penultimate) vowel is phonetically lengthened, especially in prefix-CVCV nouns, and that a HL-contoured final vowel is lengthened (>250 ms vs ~150 ms).
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; length is expressive only (ideophones written with three vowels); rising tones on short syllables are analysed as L+H sequences
new_statements.identity_note: de Wit 2010 calls the language 'Lika' (self-name [lilikó]; Glottolog 'Liko', lika1243) and states on p. 5 that it describes the central dialect (líɓó 'water'), the variety with the most speakers, distinct from the Bavágɛni (líɓá) and Bavasamba/Bavágbaka/Bevengéni (íɓó) variants and from the Nduka and Poko (Bakango) outliers. Same author and variety as the catalog's de Wit 2015 grammar.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule stated' rests on the single best description of the language: a 2015 597-pp reference grammar with a dedicated tone chapter, held locally, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited pages (121, 214, 216). A whole-text scan confirms 'stress' appears only in the Swahili/French loanword-adaptation passages (donor stress -> H tone), which the record already notes. No competing or later prosodic study exists in Glottolog's bibliography or was found online; the remaining unheld items are vowel-harmony papers and the author's own superseded sketches, so nothing is likely to change the classification. download attempts (SILEWP 2010-002 at sil.org; Kutsch Lojenga 2008 PDF at Persée) were blocked; notes
